title: Key Signatures and the Circle of Fifths
intro: Each step up a perfect fifth adds one sharp to the key signature; each step down a fifth adds one flat. Arranged in a circle, the keys show which are closely related and how far apart any two are.

blocks.text: The order of sharps and flats

Sharps always enter in the order F C G D A E B ('Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle'), each a fifth above the last. Flats enter in the reverse order, B E A D G C F. A key with three sharps has F♯, C♯ and G♯; a key with two flats has B♭ and E♭.

items: Sharp keys: the last sharp is the leading tone, so the tonic is a semitone above it. With F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ the last is D♯, so the key is E major.
Flat keys: the second-to-last flat is the tonic. With B♭ E♭ A♭ the second-to-last is E♭, so E♭ major. (F major, one flat, has to be memorised.)

blocks.alt: A circle with the twelve major keys around the outside, C at the top, then G, D, A, E, B, F♯/G♭, D♭, A♭, E♭, B♭ and F going clockwise; the relative minor keys inside (A minor under C, E minor under G and so on) and the number of sharps or flats beside each.
blocks.caption: The circle of fifths: major keys outside, relative minors inside. Clockwise is up a fifth (one more sharp or one less flat); anticlockwise is down a fifth.

items: Neighbours on the circle differ by one sharp or flat: their scales share six of seven notes. Modulating to a neighbouring key (the dominant, clockwise, or the subdominant, anticlockwise) is smooth.
Keys across the circle (C and F♯) share only two notes and are as far apart as keys get.
At the bottom the sharp and flat keys meet: F♯ major (six sharps) and G♭ major (six flats) are enharmonic. C♯ major (seven sharps) and C♭ major (seven flats) also exist and overlap D♭ and B.
Chord progressions with roots falling by fifths (iii–vi–ii–V–I) walk anticlockwise round the circle; this is the strongest kind of root motion in tonal music.

blocks.text: Why fifths: the circle doesn't quite close

Twelve perfect fifths up from C reach B♯, seven octaves higher. On a piano B♯ is C, so the circle closes. With pure 3:2 fifths it does not: $(3/2)^{12} \approx 129.75$ while $2^7 = 128$, a gap of about 23.5 cents called the Pythagorean comma. Equal temperament shrinks every fifth by 1/12 of the comma (about 2 cents) so the circle closes exactly.

config.yLabel: cents above the start (folded into one octave)

blocks.text: Each point is k pure fifths up, reduced to one octave. After 12 fifths the pure stack lands 23.46 cents above where it began, while the equal-tempered fifths come back to 0. Try 53: pure fifths come within about 3.6 cents of the start, which is why 53 equal divisions of the octave approximate Pythagorean tuning so well (see Temperaments (#/arts/music-theory/tuning/temperaments)).

blocks.title: Name the key
blocks.text: A key signature has four flats. Which major key and which minor key?
solution: Flats in order: B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭. The second-to-last is A♭, so A♭ major. Its relative minor is a minor third down: F minor.

blocks.title: Signatures
blocks.text: How many sharps or flats are in B major, D♭ major and C♯ minor?
solution: B major: five sharps (F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯). D♭ major: five flats (B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭). C♯ minor is the relative of E major: four sharps.

blocks.title: The comma
blocks.text: Show that twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves by about 23.46 cents.
solution: Twelve fifths: 12 × 1200·log2(3/2) = 12 × 701.955 = 8423.46 cents. Seven octaves: 8400 cents. Difference: 23.46 cents, the Pythagorean comma, ratio 3^12/2^19 = 531441/524288 ≈ 1.01364.
